source.title: Training a Transformer to Compose One Step Per Layer (and Proving It)

record.tranche_reason: The post tests whether models trained on the same algorithmic task learn the same identifiable algorithm, using training comparisons and mechanistic interpretability rather than measuring grokking delays.
record.gate_note: The post does not report training-versus-test accuracy over time, a post-overfitting rise, or how delay varies with training-set size. It reports algorithm-learning outcomes across task, loss, architecture, and data-weighting choices; these bear on V6. Grokking is mentioned as motivation and as inspiration for data weighting, but its characteristic accuracy trajectory is not tested.
record.test_reason: Small transformers trained on the same D3 composition task end up with different, identifiable solutions depending on loss, architecture, data weighting and seed. Mechanistic checks (logit lens, ablations) separate them: a sequential algorithm, a hybrid, or a memorized lookup table. This is direct evidence against V6. No grokking delay or accuracy trajectory is measured, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. T5 rather than T2, because the results argue the version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The author concludes that optimization pressure strongly disfavors sequential algorithms in favour of parallel solutions or memorized composed lookup tables. Universal (weight-shared) transformers, shortcut-free tasks, answer-only loss and difficulty-weighted data make sequential learning more likely, but outcomes stay seed-dependent and sensitive to task and architecture. The author also hypothesizes, untested, that full-sequence models might eventually grok the sequential algorithm with more data.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains models on D3 composition and uses logit-lens and ablation analyses to identify the learned algorithm. It does not reproduce the original grokking accuracy-versus-training trajectory or vary training-set size.
record.method_sensitivity: The learned algorithm varies with task choice, architecture/weight sharing, loss schedule, data weighting, and seed; the author warns that task and architecture choices are highly sensitive.
record.problems: The author reports seed-dependent and inconsistent outcomes, says results are sensitive to task and architecture, and notes that some experiments were not pursued because of time and cost. The post gives few numerical measurements for the algorithm-identification results and does not report uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: No train/test accuracy trajectory, delayed generalization, or training-set-size dependence measured.
Only final trained models are inspected; no training-time progress measures or memorization-removal dynamics.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning; NanoGPT/FineWeb option dropped before testing.
No weight-decay or norm analysis, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No optimizer or floating-point artifact investigated.

missing.what: Per-step critical-layer ablation detail: accuracy recovers after ablating at step t[1], and Model A appears to use a different algorithm at step t[5]. This is further evidence of within-model algorithmic heterogeneity.

record.verdict_notes: Informal LessWrong post with few numbers, no seed counts, no uncertainty, and no held-out test split described. With k=6 the 46,656 inputs may be fully enumerable, so 'memorization' here is a lookup-table solution, not overfitting. The challenge to V6 concerns which algorithm small transformers converge to on an algorithmic task, not the Fourier circuit in modular addition, and grokking dynamics are not observed. Models A and B differ only in loss schedule, which is exactly the hyperparameter-dependence V6 denies.

versions.untested_parts: No delayed test-accuracy rise, training-set-size comparison, or post-overfitting accuracy trajectory is measured.
No training-time trajectory of circuit formation or memorizing-component removal is measured; the logit lens and ablations inspect trained models.
No non-algorithmic dataset or initialization-scale/weight-norm manipulation is tested.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
No low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking below a dataset-size threshold is tested.
The post compares selected architectures, losses, and training choices on a D3 composition task, but does not establish convergence behavior across a systematic set of runs or architectures.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact is investigated.

rows.subject: standard transformers
rows.operation_detail: Train on the D3 composition task with full-sequence loss
rows.value: Standard transformers always memorized the 47k value lookup table rather than a sequential algorithm when trained this way.
rows.note: The result contrasts with sequential-algorithm learning under other training choices described in the post.

rows.subject: weight-shared transformers
rows.operation_detail: Train on the D3 composition task with answer-only loss
rows.value: Weight-shared transformers usually learned the sequential algorithm under answer-only loss.
rows.note: Contrasts with the memorizing outcome for standard transformers under full-sequence loss and with weight-shared models under full-sequence loss.

rows.subject: standard transformers
rows.operation_detail: Train on the D3 composition task with answer-only loss
rows.value: Standard transformers learned a partial sequential algorithm, compressed into the final 3 layers; this was flaky and seed-dependent.
rows.note: The reported outcome is incomplete and varies across seeds.
rows.check: Against V6 the key fact is that the outcome is 'flaky and seed-dependent'. Runs on the same task and settings reach different solutions, which runs opposite to convergence, not partial.

rows.subject: standard transformers
rows.operation_detail: Train first with answer-only loss, then with full-sequence loss

conditions.value: answer-only until 100% accuracy, then full-sequence until convergence

rows.value: When a model learned the sequential algorithm in the first phase, it consistently maintained it in the second phase; learning it in the first phase was flaky and inconsistent.
rows.note: The result is conditional on first learning the sequential algorithm.
rows.check: Retention once learned is not the V6 question. The row's bearing on V6 is that first-phase learning of the sequential algorithm is 'flaky and inconsistent' across runs.

source_check.correct: The curriculum paragraph describes a model without specifying its architecture. Sequential learning in the first phase was inconsistent; models that learned it consistently retained it during subsequent full-sequence training.
source_check.problem: The retention result is not explicitly restricted to standard transformers.

rows.subject: standard transformer
rows.operation_detail: Use difficulty-weighted data and answer-only-to-full-sequence loss curriculum
rows.value: The author was able to successfully train a standard transformer to learn the sequential algorithm, although still inconsistently.
rows.note: The author describes the result as inconsistent.
rows.check: 'Still inconsistently' means identically configured runs land on different algorithms. That contradicts V6 rather than partially showing it.

rows.subject: universal transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on the D3 composition task with answer-only loss
rows.value: It was much easier to train the universal transformer to learn the sequential algorithm, learning it in the answer-only case without data weighting.
rows.note: The post reports architecture-dependent learning outcomes.

rows.subject: weight-shared models
rows.operation_detail: Train on the D3 composition task with full-sequence loss
rows.value: Weight-shared models did not learn the sequential algorithm under full-sequence loss in the author's experiments.
rows.note: This differs from the reported answer-only outcome for weight-shared models.

rows.subject: Model A
rows.operation_detail: Inspect intermediate-state predictions with the logit lens
rows.measure: Intermediate states at operation and prediction positions across layers
rows.baseline: Chance; 17% is stated as chance for the cited comparison.
rows.value: Expected intermediate values appear at L1, L1, L3, L4, L4, and L5; the author infers sequential computation for the first 4 steps, a combined lookup table at step 5, and another sequential step at step 6.
rows.note: This identifies a hybrid algorithm rather than one uniform six-step sequential algorithm.

source_check.correct: State relative to V6: reversed in the comparison with Model B. Model A's intermediate values appear at L1, L1, L3, L4, L4 and L5; the author infers a hybrid sequential/lookup-table algorithm. The second L1 signal is 26%, versus 17% chance.

source_check.problem: Partial sequential computation is not partial support for V6; the identified algorithm differs from Model B's.

relationships.reason: Standard full-sequence training always memorizes a lookup table (R1, R7); answer-only or curriculum runs learn sequential or hybrid algorithms, inconsistently by seed (R2–R6, R8). Models A/B differ causally in logit lens and ablations (R9–R11, R14–R15).
relationships.display_finding: Full-sequence training consistently memorized lookup tables, whereas answer-only or curriculum training produced sequential or hybrid algorithms inconsistently across seeds, with Models A and B showing causal differences in logit-lens analysis and ablations.
